catalog_quote: The accent in Boondéi words falls upon the last syllable but one. Monosyllabic words are, as a rule, suffixed to the preceding word, and the accent is then thrown back, as— Mwengádu, only one, in place of Mwénga dú. The following are the most important:— -si, earth. -hya, new. -du, only. -ngwa, other people's. -ni or -i, the sign of the locative case.

new_statements.quote: The NonFinality constraints for stress and tone could be different, but the existing data provide no evidence of such a distinction. For stress, it clearly seems undominated, as stress always falls on the penultimate mora; it also seems undominated for tone as well here.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: there logs the KCI download chain. Footnote 3 is on printed p. 132 = PDF page 4 (extracted text shows the page header '132 Lee, Kent' and the footnote). The quoted sentence is there word for word: 'The NonFinality constraints for stress and tone could be different, but the existing data provide no evidence of such a distinction. For stress, it clearly seems undominated, as stress always falls on the penultimate mora; it also seems undominated for tone as well here.' The footnote hangs off the Table 3 constraint 'NonFinality[Tone]: Tone may not fall on final syllable', in the section (pp. 131-132) arguing that prefixal H tones shift rightward under Align-R(Tone, PWd) but surface on the penul…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (penultimate). Adds the mora-based wording ('penultimate mora'), the undominated NonFinality account, the statement that Kibondei is a tone language (H vs toneless) with tone also surfacing on the penult, and the emphatic-stress override in reduplication. Data come from a single native-speaker informant recorded at UIUC in the mid-1990s.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress always falls on the penultimate mora (in practice the penultimate syllable; no vowel-length contrast is discussed). The language is otherwise tonal: lexical/prefixal high tones shift rightward within the prosodic word and surface on the penult because a NonFinality constraint bans final-syllable tone (pp. 131-132); the same NonFinality holds for stress. The stress statement is a footnote aside, not a dedicated section.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 146: in contrastively emphatic reduplicated forms an initial high tone is interpreted as a marker of 'emphatic stress' that 'overrides the lexical stresses' and is copied into the reduplicant; the author flags this as a discourse-level effect needing study in conversational data. No lexical exceptions to penultimate stress are given.
new_statements.identity_note: Lee 2013 describes Kibondei (Kibondéi, Bondei) of northeastern Tanzania, elicited from one native-speaker informant (a graduate student at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in the mid-1990s); no dialect is named. This is the same language as catalog Boondéi (bond1247).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on the page image we hold of Woodward 1882 p. 2; C&K ROA-176 (held) supports only the tone note. (2) Deciding source is an 1882 missionary grammar sketch; it is old but by the acknowledged authority of the time, and nothing later contradicts it: Meinhof 1906 (downloaded now from archive.org, MSOS Jg. IX pp. 278-284) is silent on accent and defers to Woodward; modern tonal work (C&K 1997/98. Lamont 2025 downloaded, open access) shows H-tone barred from final position and shifted to the penult plus phrase-penultimate vowel lengthening, i.e. right-edge penultimate prominence consistent with the trochaic-penult coding, though framed at the phrase level as in Swahili-type NE Coastal Bantu.
